In answer to the Attorney General (Sri L. Carson) Mr. Booth said that after the rush of homeward-bound Americans was over—it was towards the end of October—it became a question as to whether they could continue running the two large steamers, the Lusitania and Mauretania, at all.

"We went into the matter very carefully, and we came to the conclusion that it would be possible to continue running one of them at a reduced speed; that is to say, the traffic would be sufficient, but only sufficient to justify running one steamer a month if we reduced the expenses."
"No steamer over fourteen knots had, as far as I know, been struck by a submarine."
The Attorney-General: To run at a profit?—To pay expenses. We did not expect to make a profit and, in fact, we did not make a profit.
They decided, he added, to run the Lusitania at three-quarters boiler power, and that meant a reduction of speed from an average of about twenty-four knots to an average of about twenty-one knots.

"have not referred to anything in particular," said the Attorney-General. "I want to know whether you had any information that threats were made of her being attacked by submarines on this particular voyage?"

Witness: I do not think that I heard anything about special threats made in New York until the Sunday morning after the Lusitania had sailed, but I understand that the threats were published in New York on the Saturday morning. Therefore I do not think I could have heard until Saturday afternoon at the earliest.
"But before that," asked the Attorney-General, "had you any information of submarines being on the route in which the ships were travelling?"
Mr. Booth replied in the affirmative.

"May I take it," asked the Attorney-General, "that at the time the boat left New York you were fully alive to the importance of the factor of steam in relation to the journey so as to avoid a submarine disaster?"

"That being so, do you tell his Lordship that you had no consultation as to whether, having regard to that factor, you should not increase the speed for 'he journeys by using the five other boilers?'"

Mr. Booth's reply was: "That question, if it had arisen at all, would have arisen in February, when the first submarine attacks were made, and my view was, or the view of my directors was, that the Lusitania, being in fact the fastest ship running, the difference between twenty-one and twenty-four knots was not material so far as avoiding submarines was concerned.
